analysis.one_liner: Expands whistleblower lawsuits against contractors and others who submit false claims for federal money.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill on a bipartisan basis in July 2008 and placed it on the Senate's calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The False Claims Act lets private citizens (whistleblowers) sue on the government's behalf when someone bills the government fraudulently, and recover a share of whatever the government gets back. This bill closed several loopholes that had been limiting those suits: it made people liable for false claims routed through contractors and grantees rather than directly to a government employee, gave anti-retaliation protection to contractor employees, not just federal workers, set a 10-year window for bringing cases, and made it harder for fraud claims to be waived away in private settlements.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who fund the programs the bill protects; whistleblowers, who would get stronger protection and clearer rights to a share of recoveries; and federal and state treasuries, which recover triple damages from fraudsters.

how_it_helps.text: Makes a person liable for false claims even when the claim is presented to a contractor or grantee of a federal program rather than directly to a government employee, closing a loophole courts had used to dismiss fraud cases [S3][S4].
Extends protection against firing or demotion for reporting fraud to government contractors and agents, not just federal employees, with double back pay and reinstatement [S3][S4].
Sets a 10-year time limit for bringing a false claims case and lets the government's later complaint relate back to the whistleblower's original filing date [S3][S4].
Prevents false-claim liability from being waived or released outside a court-approved settlement, so private deals cannot wipe out fraud claims [S3][S4].
Lets Department of Justice designees issue civil investigative demands and share investigative information with whistleblowers, speeding up fraud probes [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Contractors, grantees, health care providers, and other recipients of federal money who submit false claims, who would face broader liability, higher penalties adjusted for inflation, and court costs; in the long run, the cost of any increased litigation flows through federal procurement.

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise the stakes for any entity doing business with the government: penalties would be inflation-adjusted and the bill covers 'reckless disregard' without proof of intent to defraud, which contractors argued invites costly suits over honest billing errors [S4].

The bill also trims whistleblower rights in some places: courts may reduce a whistleblower's share of the proceeds if the information came mainly from a government disclosure, the government can move to dismiss certain relators who are federal employees or their family members, and the reported version would dismiss suits based largely on matters already in criminal proceedings, news reports, or congressional investigations unless the whistleblower added substantial new grounds for recovery [S3][S4].

Broader liability and a longer 10-year filing window could increase defense and litigation costs for companies that do business with the government, costs that ultimately show up in contract pricing [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main effect is to make it easier to recover public money lost to fraud and to protect the people who report it, at a cost borne almost entirely by entities that submitted false claims, plus some litigation friction for honest contractors. Its own drafting acknowledged the tradeoff by adding government power to dismiss weak or duplicative whistleblower suits. The core expansion — covering claims routed through contractors and protecting contractor employees — addresses loopholes that had let real fraud cases be thrown out.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved it with an amendment and put it on the Senate's waiting list in July 2008, but nobody brought it to the floor for a vote before the session ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Sen. Grassley on September 12, 2007 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S1][S6].
The committee held hearings in February 2008 and ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment on April 3, 2008 [S6].
Sen. Leahy reported the bill to the Senate with an amendment on July 29, 2008, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 910 [S4][S6].
A written committee report was filed on September 25, 2008 (Report No. 110-507), but the Senate never held a floor vote on the bill, and the 110th Congress ended January 3, 2009 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government contractors and other recipients of federal funds facing potential fraud suits are better off, since the loopholes the bill would have closed stayed open; whistleblowers and the Treasury gained nothing from this effort.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks; had earlier championed the 1986 False Claims Act amendments

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill to the Senate with an amendment, placed it on the Senate calendar, and filed the written committee report

for.name: Sens. Durbin, Leahy, Specter, and Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support from the start

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, adding Republican support

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote despite its placement on the legislative calendar; the bill died at the end of the session

against.name: Federal contractor and health care industry groups
against.role: Opposition lobbying against False Claims Act expansion
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against strengthening qui tam liability and penalties for government contractors; the bill's provisions narrowing some whistleblower rights reflect the negotiated compromises with these interests

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican (Grassley) with 3 Democratic and 1 Republican cosponsors, and was reported out of the Democratic-led Judiciary Committee favorably; there is no record of floor opposition votes because it never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Federal contractors and grantees (defense, health care, and other government vendors)
industries.note: The bill would have closed loopholes letting these entities escape False Claims Act liability when false claims go through subcontractors or grantees, and raised penalties adjusted for inflation. Their gain from the bill dying is avoided triple damages and a longer reach for whistleblower suits.

industries.industry: Whistleblower plaintiffs (qui tam relators) and the lawyers who represent them
industries.note: The bill strengthens and clarifies whistleblower awards in most respects (10-year window, retaliation protection for contractor employees, anti-waiver language) but narrows awards for relators who derive their claims from public disclosures or government investigations, and lets DOJ dismiss certain federal-employee relators.

The bill expands DOJ's investigative tools (civil investigative demand delegation, information sharing with relators) and gives the government explicit power to remove certain relators, making enforcement more efficient while keeping control in DOJ hands.
